# Tracking tissue loss after ischemia {#sec-linear-regression-single-continuous}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)

# The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)
Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

# Read the cell data and treat the day as a number
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI <- as.numeric(cell_data$DPI)

# Number formatters used in the text: one and two decimals
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
```

Remember the question from the lab meeting: not "does it go up?" but *how much, per day, and how sure are you?* So far we have answered only half of it. @sec-linear-regression-what gave us the words for the answer (an intercept, a slope, a leftover), and @sec-linear-regression-assumptions told us, with some embarrassment, that the line we drew across the whole 30 days of the ischemia study does not deserve our trust. It failed linearity and equal spread for a reason that is biological: an early bump at day 3, followed by a decline that flattens after day 14. In my experience with cerebral ischemia, the injured brain first goes through an inflammatory phase that lasts from one to five days, depending on how large the lesion is, and the hemisphere swells during it. What follows is a long atrophy, with progressive loss of tissue. Inflammation first, atrophy after: that is the general course of the injury, and a straight line has no way to represent a rise followed by a fall. This chapter keeps the promise made there. We shrink the window to where a straight line is an honest description, fit it with both lenses, and finally put a number with a margin around it on *how much tissue is lost per day*.

## The full range, once more

Before cutting anything, I want you to see what we are cutting. `DPI` takes only five values, so a plain scatter stacks the animals into five columns. The honest way to look is to nudge the points sideways a little, mark each day's mean, and draw the straight line the previous chapters fitted across everything (@fig-single_continuous_full_range). `geom_jitter()` does the nudging, and each day's mean is a diamond (`geom_point(shape = 18)`); a bar of means would have hidden the bump at day 3 and the spread inside every day. If that line were a good summary, the means would sit on it. (I left out the marginal histograms from the EDA chapters: for `DPI` they would only show five spikes.)

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_full_range
#| fig-cap: "Tissue area by day after ischemia, with the straight line fitted across all days. Orange diamonds mark each day's mean; the shaded band is the window we keep."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

# Mean tissue area per day, kept as a named vector for the text below
means_full <- aggregate(Tissue_Area ~ DPI, data = cell_data, FUN = mean)
m <- setNames(means_full$Tissue_Area, means_full$DPI)

# Every animal (jittered), the line fitted across all days, and each day's mean
# as an orange diamond; the shaded band is the window we keep
ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 3, xmax = 14, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.4, height = 0, color = "grey35", alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = means_full, shape = 18, size = 5, color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme
```

The diamonds tell the story the line cannot. Mean tissue area goes from `r f1(m["0"])` mm² at day 0 (the shams) up to `r f1(m["3"])` at day 3, then down through `r f1(m["7"])` and `r f1(m["14"])`, and ends at `r f1(m["30"])` by day 30, where the decline has flattened. A single slope has to split the difference between a rise, a fall and a plateau, so it is too high for some days and too low for others. That is not a flaw of this dataset. It is what happens whenever a biological process changes character partway along the axis you are modeling, and the inflammation-then-atrophy arc of cerebral ischemia does exactly that.

## Keeping the stretch where a line is honest

The shaded band marks the stretch I keep: days 3, 7 and 14, the three days with a decline and nothing else going on (@fig-single-continuous-frame). I also drop the sham animals, since they exist only at day 0 and would sneak a condition contrast into what should be a pure time slope.

![Through the frame the path is straight; outside it, it bends. A straight line is honest only over the stretch you frame, and I framed this one after looking at the whole path.](images/linear-regression-single-continuous_frame-on-straight-stretch.png){#fig-single-continuous-frame fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a dirt path over rolling green hills that climbs into a bump on the left, descends in a nearly straight line through an empty wooden picture frame standing on the path, then flattens out to the right under a pale blue sky."}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-single_continuous_days
#| tbl-cap: Tissue area by day within the DPI 3 to 14 window

library(gt)

# Keep days 3, 7 and 14, and centre the day at 3 (so day 3 becomes zero)
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, DPI %in% c(3, 7, 14))
cell_data_sub$DPI_c <- cell_data_sub$DPI - 3

# Animals, mean and SD of tissue area for each day of the window
day_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cell_data_sub, cell_data_sub$DPI), function(d) {
  data.frame(DPI = d$DPI[1], Animals = nrow(d),
             Mean = mean(d$Tissue_Area), SD = sd(d$Tissue_Area))
}))

# Show the day summary as a table
gt(day_summary) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Mean, SD), decimals = 2)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Mean loss per day in each stretch, for the text below
drop_3_7 <- (day_summary$Mean[1] - day_summary$Mean[2]) / 4
drop_7_14 <- (day_summary$Mean[2] - day_summary$Mean[3]) / 7
```

Two things in @tbl-single_continuous_days matter. First, the loss per day is close to the same in both stretches: about `r f2(drop_3_7)` mm² per day between days 3 and 7 and `r f2(drop_7_14)` between days 7 and 14. That is exactly what a straight line claims, and it is why this window is defensible. Second, there is one row per animal (`r day_summary$Animals[1]`, `r day_summary$Animals[2]` and `r day_summary$Animals[3]` animals per day), so the independence assumption from @sec-linear-regression-assumptions is not the worry here. The worry is in the last column: the spread at day 3 is visibly larger than at days 7 and 14. We will come back to it, because it is going to matter.

::: callout-tip
### I chose this window after looking at the data

I picked days 3 to 14 *after* seeing the means in @fig-single_continuous_full_range. That is a decision made with the data in hand, and a different analyst might have drawn the window elsewhere. So the slope below is a statement about this stretch of the time course, not a law of ischemia. The honest way to cover the whole 30 days is not to keep trimming until a line fits, but to use a model that can bend, which is what @sec-longitudinal-timeseries does.
:::

## Writing the model down

Running this regression answers the same question this book keeps coming back to:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***What's the value of knowing A if I know B?***
:::

Here $B$ is the number of days since ischemia, and $A$ is hemispheric tissue area. How much does knowing the day tell us about the area? The model has the shape you already know, with one change I will explain in a moment:

$$
\text{Area}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot (\text{DPI}_i - 3) + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
$$ {#eq-single-continuous}

$\text{Area}_i$ is the tissue area of animal $i$ and $\text{DPI}_i$ its measurement day, both real, numeric, continuous variables (unlike the categorical `Condition` of @sec-intro-applied-modeling). $\beta_1$ is the slope: how much area changes per additional day. $\epsilon_i$ is everything else, same as always.

The change is the "$-3$". In @eq-linear-regression-simple, $\beta_0$ is the value of $y$ when $x = 0$, and here $x = 0$ is day 0, the one day this window leaves out. The model would happily extrapolate to a day it never saw, and the answer would be a number that nobody can check against anything. Think of it as setting the zero of a ruler (@fig-single-continuous-zero). You can put the zero where the table of measurements ends, or at the start of the stretch you actually measured. Centering `DPI` at day 3 does the second: $\beta_0$ becomes the expected area *at day 3*, a number we can hold up against the animals we really measured. It costs nothing, because shifting $x$ changes only the intercept and leaves the slope untouched (see @tbl-single_continuous_centering).

![Where you put the zero of the ruler is up to you. Putting it at the start of the stretch you measured gives an intercept you can check against real animals.](images/linear-regression-single-continuous_sliding-the-zero.png){#fig-single-continuous-zero fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of two wooden rulers on a bench, one above the other. Three small stones sit along the top ruler, which has a teal flag at its far left end; the lower ruler is slid to the right so that an ochre flag marks its zero at the first stone, joined by a dashed line."}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-single_continuous_centering
#| tbl-cap: Centering DPI at day 3 moves the intercept into the data and leaves the slope alone

# Same line fitted twice: with the raw day, and with the day centred at 3
coef_raw <- coef(lm(Tissue_Area ~ DPI, data = cell_data_sub))
coef_cen <- coef(lm(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_c, data = cell_data_sub))

# Compare the two intercepts and slopes
gt(data.frame(
  Version = c("DPI (zero = day 0, outside the window)", "DPI minus 3 (zero = day 3, inside the window)"),
  Intercept = c(coef_raw[[1]], coef_cen[[1]]),
  Slope = c(coef_raw[[2]], coef_cen[[2]])
)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Intercept, Slope), decimals = 2)
```

The uncentered intercept, `r f1(coef_raw[[1]])` mm², is higher than anything we measured in sham animals at day 0 (`r f1(m["0"])` mm²), because it extrapolates a line fitted on the way down from the day-3 bump. The centered intercept, `r f1(coef_cen[[1]])` mm², sits where the data are.

## What I believed before looking

@sec-priors-regularization taught us that leaving a prior at its default is a decision, so this time I make it on purpose. In my own data and in the ischemia models I have worked with before, hemispheric tissue shrinks on the order of 1 mm² per day through the first two weeks. That number comes from my experience and my earlier data, not from a paper, and I would rather say so than dress it up. So the slope prior is centered at $-1$ mm² per day, with a small spread: a standard deviation of 0.5 mm² per day. Written on the scale of the outcome, that prior says three things. A loss of 2 mm² per day sustained over 11 days would remove more tissue than any section in this file contains (the largest is `r f1(max(cell_data$Tissue_Area))` mm²), and the prior gives it little weight. A *gain* is nearly ruled out, since only about `r round(100 * (1 - pnorm(0, -1, 0.5)))`% of the prior probability sits above zero. And everything between no change and a loss of 2 mm² per day is allowed to compete (@tbl-single_continuous_priors).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-single_continuous_priors
#| tbl-cap: Priors for the tissue-loss model, with their reading on the scale of the outcome

# Smallest and largest section in the file, to ground the priors
area_range <- range(cell_data$Tissue_Area)

# The three priors and what each means on the scale of tissue area
gt(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Intercept (area at day 3)", "Slope (mm² per day)", "sigma (spread around the line)"),
  Prior = c("Normal(15, 4)", "Normal(-1, 0.5)", "Exponential(0.5)"),
  Reading = c(
    sprintf("95%% of belief between 7 and 23 mm²; the sections in this file run from %.1f to %.1f mm²", area_range[1], area_range[2]),
    "About 95% of belief between a loss of 2 mm² per day and no change",
    sprintf("Mean of 2 mm²; only %.0f%% of belief above 6 mm², an implausible typical distance from the line when areas run from %.1f to %.1f mm²", 100 * exp(-0.5 * 6), area_range[1], area_range[2])
  )
))
```

The intercept and `sigma` priors are deliberately loose; they only keep the sampler away from absurd regions (areas of 100 mm², say). Only the slope carries real prior knowledge, and the sensitivity check below tells us how much that knowledge changes the answer. One `brms` detail: by default it places the intercept prior on a version of the intercept with the predictors centered at their mean, which here would be day 8.7, not day 3. Writing `0 + Intercept` in the formula puts the prior on the intercept we actually named.

## Fitting it twice

A plain `lm()` gives us the likelihood-only answer: the same line a flat prior would produce, with an interval that cannot use anything we knew beforehand. `brms` fits the same linear model but hands back the full posterior for every quantity we care about, including derived ones (we will compute the percentage lost between days 3 and 14 in a moment), and lets the prior in the table above enter the calculation. Putting the two side by side is also how we see what the prior did.

```{r}
library(brms)

# The three priors from the table above
priors <- c(
  prior(normal(15, 4), class = b, coef = Intercept),
  prior(normal(-1, 0.5), class = b, coef = DPI_c),
  prior(exponential(0.5), class = sigma)
)

# 0 + Intercept puts the intercept prior on the intercept at day 3;
# sample_prior = "yes" also keeps draws from the prior for the overlay figure
brms_model <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ 0 + Intercept + DPI_c,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  prior = priors,
  sample_prior = "yes",
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-single-continuous_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

library(posterior)

# All posterior draws, and the sampler checks for the three parameters
draws <- as_draws_df(brms_model)
conv <- summarise_draws(
  subset_draws(draws, variable = c("b_Intercept", "b_DPI_c", "sigma")),
  "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail"
)
n_div <- sum(subset(nuts_params(brms_model), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

# Quantities derived draw by draw: slope, intercept, area at day 14 (11 days later)
# and the percentage lost between day 3 and day 14
slope <- draws$b_DPI_c
icpt <- draws$b_Intercept
pred14 <- icpt + 11 * slope
drop_pct <- 100 * (1 - pred14 / icpt)

# Helper: the middle 95% of a set of draws
ci <- function(x) quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
# Posterior summaries, Rhat and effective sample sizes
summary(brms_model)
```

The sampler did its job: the largest Rhat is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(conv$rhat))` (under the 1.01 threshold), the smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes are `r format(round(min(conv$ess_bulk)), big.mark = ",")` and `r format(round(min(conv$ess_tail)), big.mark = ",")` (well past 400), and there are `r n_div` divergent transitions. That vouches for the *sampling*, which is a separate question from whether the *model* describes the biology; we get to that at the end.

### parsnip

```{r}
library(parsnip)
library(broom)

# The same line by ordinary least squares, with 95% confidence intervals
parsnip_model <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  fit(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_c, data = cell_data_sub)

tidy(parsnip_model, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

## Reading the coefficients

The slope is about $`r f2(median(slope))`$ mm² per day (95% credible interval $`r f2(ci(slope)[1])`$ to $`r f2(ci(slope)[2])`$): for each additional day inside this window, hemispheric area falls by roughly two thirds of a square millimeter. The intercept says an animal at day 3 is expected to have about `r f1(median(icpt))` mm² (95% credible interval `r f1(ci(icpt)[1])` to `r f1(ci(icpt)[2])`), close to the `r f1(day_summary$Mean[1])` mm² we actually averaged at day 3. That is the check the uncentered intercept could not offer. And because we hold the whole posterior, any quantity built from the parameters comes with its own uncertainty for free: computed draw by draw, the expected area at day 14 is `r f1(median(pred14))` mm², a loss of about `r round(median(drop_pct))`% over eleven days (95% credible interval `r round(ci(drop_pct)[1])`% to `r round(ci(drop_pct)[2])`%).

A table of coefficients is easy to read past, so let me draw the line itself (@fig-single_continuous_fit). I show the uncertainty as nested bands (50%, 80% and 95%, drawn with `stat_lineribbon()` from the `ggdist` package) instead of a single hard-edged interval, so the eye reads a gradient of plausibility rather than a boundary. One caution about what the bands are: they describe our uncertainty about the *average* tissue area at each day, not about where an individual animal will land, which is far wider.

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_fit
#| fig-cap: Posterior mean line for tissue area against days post-ischemia (50%, 80% and 95% credible bands), with the animals behind it
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

library(ggdist)

# 50 days between 3 and 14, and the expected area at each one for every posterior draw
grid <- data.frame(DPI = seq(3, 14, length.out = 50))
grid$DPI_c <- grid$DPI - 3
mu <- posterior_epred(brms_model, newdata = grid)

# One row per (day, draw)
line_draws <- data.frame(DPI = rep(grid$DPI, each = nrow(mu)), mu = c(mu))

# Mean line with nested 50%, 80% and 95% bands, and the animals behind it
ggplot(line_draws, aes(x = DPI, y = mu)) +
  stat_lineribbon(.width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), linewidth = 0.8, color = "#0072B2") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  geom_jitter(data = cell_data_sub, aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area),
              width = 0.25, height = 0, color = "grey25", alpha = 0.7, size = 2,
              inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(3, 7, 14)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)", fill = "Credible level") +
  Plot_theme
```

## How far did the data move us?

A prior is only honest if you show how much it mattered. @fig-single_continuous_prior_posterior overlays what I believed before looking (dashed) and what I believe after (solid) for the slope.

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_prior_posterior
#| fig-cap: Prior and posterior for the slope (mm² per day)
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

# Stack prior draws and posterior draws of the slope
overlay <- data.frame(
  slope = c(draws$prior_b_DPI_c, draws$b_DPI_c),
  distribution = rep(c("Prior", "Posterior"), each = nrow(draws))
)

# Prior (dashed) and posterior (solid); labels sit on the curves, so no legend
ggplot(overlay, aes(x = slope, color = distribution, linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Prior = "#E69F00", Posterior = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.85, y = 0.5, label = "Prior", color = "#E69F00", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.45, y = 4.2, label = "Posterior", color = "#0072B2", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "Slope: change in tissue area per day (mm²/day)", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none()
```

The data did most of the work. A prior centered at $-1$ with a standard deviation of 0.5 became a posterior centered near $`r f2(median(slope))`$ with a standard deviation of about `r f2(sd(slope))`, several times narrower and shifted toward what the `r nrow(cell_data_sub)` animals say. My prior expected a slightly steeper loss than the animals show, and the data corrected it without a fight. The formal version of that check is to refit under a visibly different prior and ask whether the conclusion survives. I use a skeptical one, centered on *no effect*:

```{r}
# Refit with a skeptical prior centred on no effect, to test sensitivity
brms_skeptic <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ 0 + Intercept + DPI_c,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(15, 4), class = b, coef = Intercept),
    prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b, coef = DPI_c),
    prior(exponential(0.5), class = sigma)
  ),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-single-continuous_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-single_continuous_sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: The slope under three analyses (mm² per day)

# Median and 95% interval of a set of slope draws, as one table row
slope_row <- function(x, label) {
  q <- unname(quantile(x, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975)))
  data.frame(Analysis = label, Estimate = q[1], Lower = q[2], Upper = q[3])
}
# The least-squares slope, then all three analyses in one table
lm_slope <- tidy(parsnip_model, conf.int = TRUE)
lm_slope <- lm_slope[lm_slope$term == "DPI_c", ]

sens <- rbind(
  slope_row(slope, "brms, informed prior Normal(-1, 0.5)"),
  slope_row(as_draws_df(brms_skeptic)$b_DPI_c, "brms, skeptical prior Normal(0, 0.5)"),
  data.frame(Analysis = "parsnip (lm), no prior", Estimate = lm_slope$estimate,
             Lower = lm_slope$conf.low, Upper = lm_slope$conf.high)
)

gt(sens) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Estimate, Lower, Upper), decimals = 2)
```

The conclusion does not depend on my prior. Even a prior that starts from *no effect* ends within a few hundredths of the others (@tbl-single_continuous_sensitivity), so the data, not my experience, carry this inference. That is worth knowing, because with other datasets it will not always be true.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** Within the window from day 3 to day 14 after ischemia, hemispheric tissue area fell by `r f2(abs(median(slope)))` mm² per day (95% credible interval `r f2(abs(ci(slope)[2]))` to `r f2(abs(ci(slope)[1]))`). Expected area was `r f1(median(icpt))` mm² at day 3 and `r f1(median(pred14))` mm² at day 14, a loss of about `r round(median(drop_pct))`% (95% credible interval `r round(ci(drop_pct)[1])`% to `r round(ci(drop_pct)[2])`%).

**Methods.** We fitted a Gaussian linear model in `brms` with the day centered at 3, so the intercept is the area at day 3. The slope prior was Normal(-1, 0.5) mm² per day, based on earlier work in this model; the intercept and the residual standard deviation had weakly informative priors. Replacing the slope prior with a skeptical Normal(0, 0.5) changed the estimated slope by `r f2(max(sens$Estimate) - min(sens$Estimate))` mm² per day across the three analyses. Sampler diagnostics were clean (largest Rhat `r sprintf("%.3f", max(conv$rhat))`, no divergent transitions). A posterior predictive check showed a single residual spread is too wide for days 7 and 14 and too narrow for day 3, so intervals for individual animals should not be read from this model.
:::

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

`brms` and `lm` agree to the second decimal, and now we can say why. With `r nrow(cell_data_sub)` animals the likelihood is far sharper than my prior: the prior carries only about `r round(100 * (1 / 0.5^2) / ((1 / 0.5^2) + (1 / lm_slope$std.error^2)), 1)`% of the weight in the slope, so the posterior is almost exactly what `lm` maximizes on its own [@gelman2020]. The `lm` row is also, in effect, the answer a flat prior would give, so the table doubles as a check against the fully noncommittal analysis. The divergence you will see later in the book shows up with hierarchical structure, tiny samples, or priors that do real regularizing work; none of those applies yet to this single-level model.
:::

## Is the line honest about the spread?

Now the promise I made at the table of days: the spread at day 3. The model has one `sigma` for the whole window, so it assumes every animal scatters around the line by the same amount. @fig-single_continuous_residuals checks that, as @sec-linear-regression-assumptions taught us to: not with a test, with a picture.

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_residuals
#| fig-cap: Residuals of the tissue-loss model by day (mm²)
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

# Residual of every animal (posterior mean prediction subtracted), by day
resid_df <- data.frame(
  DPI = factor(cell_data_sub$DPI),
  residual = residuals(brms_model)[, "Estimate"]
)

# Spread per day, and the day-3 spread without its single lowest animal
res_sd <- tapply(resid_df$residual, resid_df$DPI, sd)
res3 <- resid_df$residual[resid_df$DPI == "3"]
res3_sd_trimmed <- sd(res3[res3 > min(res3)])

# Every residual as a point; the dashed line at zero marks a perfect prediction
ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = DPI, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Residual (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme
```

The residuals at day 3 spread with a standard deviation of about `r f1(res_sd["3"])` mm², against `r f1(res_sd["7"])` at day 7 and `r f1(res_sd["14"])` at day 14. Subsetting fixed what it was meant to fix, the linearity, but not this. Part of the day-3 spread is one animal about `r f1(abs(min(res3)))` mm² below the line (the lone low point in @fig-single_continuous_fit), and with eight animals a single unusual mouse and a genuinely wider day are hard to tell apart. Without that animal the day-3 standard deviation falls to `r f1(res3_sd_trimmed)` mm², still well above the `r f1(res_sd["14"])` to `r f1(res_sd["7"])` of the other days, so some of the excess is a genuinely wider day and some is one unusual mouse, and with eight animals I cannot say how much is which. The single `sigma` (`r f1(median(draws$sigma))` mm²) averages over a noisy day 3 and two calm days, so it is too large for days 7 and 14 and too small for day 3 as we observed it. The slope itself is not in question, since its credible interval sits far from zero, but I would not trust the model to predict where a *new* day-3 animal will land. The direct fix is to let `sigma` depend on the day, a distributional model, which is what @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression does; @sec-appendix-assumption-tests shows what that change does on the full-range data.

@sec-mcmc-model-checking introduced the posterior predictive check as the way to ask whether a fitted model's simulated data resemble the real thing. A density overlay would not show the day-3 problem, so I check the quantity that matters: for each day, the standard deviation of the observed animals against the standard deviations of datasets the model replicated (@fig-single_continuous_ppcheck). The figure comes from `ppc_stat_grouped()` in `bayesplot`, which lets you pick the statistic and the grouping; choosing the statistic you are worried about is what makes a posterior predictive check informative.

```{r}
#| label: fig-single_continuous_ppcheck
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive check of the standard deviation by day (observed value as a line, replicated datasets as histograms)
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

library(bayesplot)

# 500 replicated datasets from the fitted model
yrep <- posterior_predict(brms_model, ndraws = 500)

# Per day: SD of the real animals (line) against SDs of the replicated datasets (bars)
ppc_stat_grouped(
  y = cell_data_sub$Tissue_Area,
  yrep = yrep,
  group = factor(cell_data_sub$DPI),
  stat = "sd"
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Observed SD per day, and how often a replicated dataset scatters at least that much
obs_sd <- tapply(cell_data_sub$Tissue_Area, cell_data_sub$DPI, sd)
share_as_large <- sapply(names(obs_sd), function(d) {
  idx <- cell_data_sub$DPI == as.numeric(d)
  mean(apply(yrep[, idx], 1, sd) >= obs_sd[[d]])
})
```

The two ends of the figure pull in opposite directions, which is what a single `sigma` forces. At day 3 the observed standard deviation (`r f1(obs_sd["3"])` mm²) sits in the far right tail of what the model replicates: only about `r round(100 * share_as_large["3"])`% of replicated datasets scatter that much at day 3. At days 7 and 14 the observed values (`r f1(obs_sd["7"])` and `r f1(obs_sd["14"])` mm²) sit at the left edge, with about `r round(100 * mean(share_as_large[c("7", "14")]))`% of replicates scattering at least that much at each of them, because the model expects about `r f1(median(draws$sigma))` mm² everywhere. The model's one `sigma` is a compromise that is wrong in both directions. A density overlay would have looked fine and missed all of this, which is why the check should be built around the thing you suspect.

Two coefficients, an honestly scoped window, a prior I can defend and a named limitation: that is a complete linear regression, start to finish. @sec-linear-regression-multiple picks up the natural next question: what happens once we bring a second predictor into this same model? And further out, @sec-longitudinal-timeseries returns to the *entire* 0 to 30 day range we set aside, this time with a model built to represent a rise followed by a fall, instead of subsetting the problem away.
